claims.claim: Infection control is the set of practices that prevents or stops the spread of infections in healthcare settings (CDC working definition).

An infection occurs when germs enter the body, increase in number, and cause a reaction in the body; three elements must be present: a source of germs, a susceptible person, and a way for germs to travel.

Healthcare patients are often especially susceptible: underlying conditions (e.g., diabetes, cancer, organ transplantation), certain medications (e.g., antibiotics, steroids, some cancer treatments), and devices or procedures (urinary catheters, IV lines, surgery) increase infection risk by weakening defenses or giving germs extra doorways.

Germs do not move themselves; in healthcare settings they travel by contact (touching), sprays and splashes, inhalation, and sharps injuries, carried by people, the environment, and medical equipment.

CDC organizes protection into two tiers of precautions: standard precautions for all patient care (risk assessment, common-sense practices, PPE) and transmission-based precautions added when a patient has a known or suspected infection.

CDC's core practices required in all healthcare settings include hand hygiene, environmental cleaning and disinfection, injection and medication safety, risk-assessment-based use of personal protective equipment, respiratory hygiene and cough etiquette, and reprocessing of reusable equipment.

Infection prevention and control protects both patients and health workers: WHO describes it as a practical, evidence-based approach preventing patients and health workers from being harmed by avoidable infections, and CDC describes reducing infection risk among healthcare workers, patients, and visitors.

Effective infection prevention and control requires constant action at all levels of the health system, including policymakers, facility managers, health workers, and people who access health services.
Much of the work of infection prevention and control is hidden, because it prevents problems rather than treating them after the fact.

Vaccination reduces susceptibility: a susceptible person is defined by CDC as someone who is not vaccinated or otherwise immune, and vaccines teach the immune system to recognize specific germs without the dangers of a full infection.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is infection control primarily about protecting patients or about protecting healthcare workers?
positions: Patient-safety framings emphasize preventing infections that patients acquire during care.
Occupational framings emphasize protecting healthcare personnel from exposure (CDC maintains dedicated occupationally-acquired infection resources).
WHO and CDC frame the two as simultaneous: the same practices prevent harm to patients and health workers.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the dual-protection framing (patients AND staff), which is the explicit wording of both WHO's IPC definition and CDC's mission statement for infection control. The original example shows the same practices protecting both sides.

sourceRecords.title: How Infections Spread
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), National Center for Emerging and Zoonotic Infectious Diseases
sourceRecords.notes: Read via Wayback Machine capture 20230601000000 of the canonical CDC URL (content now served under /infection-control/hcp/how-infections-spread/). Supports: germs are part of everyday life and only a small portion cause infection; an infection occurs when germs enter the body, multiply, and cause a reaction; the three required elements (source, susceptible person, transmission); sources in healthcare (patients, healthcare workers, visitors; dry surfaces such as bed rails, medical equipment, countertops; wet surfaces and sinks; indwelling devices such as catheters and IV lines); susceptibility factors (underlying conditions such as diabetes, cancer, organ transplantation; certain medications including antibiotics, steroids, and some cancer treatments; urinary catheters, tubes, and surgery as doorways); transmission routes (contact, sprays and splashes, inhalation, sharps injuries); and 'germs don't move themselves.' Facts synthesized in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: CDC's Core Infection Prevention and Control Practices for Safe Healthcare Delivery in All Settings
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), Healthcare Infection Control Practices Advisory Committee (HICPAC)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via Wayback Machine capture 20230601000000 of the canonical CDC URL (HICPAC core practices; originally approved July 2014, updated October 2022). Supports: a core set of infection prevention and control practices required in all healthcare settings; standard precautions for all patients in all settings include hand hygiene, environmental cleaning and disinfection, injection and medication safety, risk-assessment-based use of PPE (gloves, gowns, face masks), minimizing potential exposures (respiratory hygiene and cough etiquette), and reprocessing of reusable medical equipment. Used for the layers-of-defense one-liners and the cleaning-as-named-practice point. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.
